Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. For the weak formulation, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and the restricted Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, almost-everywhere equality and integral conventions of the conservative weak-form definition. These conventions concern the weak initial data. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$ measured in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

Let $h,a,\rho_0,\mu>0$, let $p_0,G,V_0,V_1\in\mathbb R$, and set $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. In the constant-density model

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$

take the infinite plane channel $\Omega_{\rm ch}=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ 0<y<h,\ z\in\mathbb R\}$, with $u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, $v\in C^2([0,h])$, and wall values $v(0)=V_0$, $v(h)=V_1$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$v(y)=V_0+(V_1-V_0)\frac yh+\frac{G}{2\mu}y(h-y).$$

Its volume flux per unit width in the $z$ direction and its fixed-coordinate shear component are

$$Q_{\rm ch}=\int_0^h v(y)\,dy=\frac h2(V_0+V_1)+\frac{Gh^3}{12\mu},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(0)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}+\frac{Gh}{2},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(h)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}-\frac{Gh}{2}.$$

For the infinite circular pipe $\Omega_a=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ y^2+z^2<a^2\}$, take $x$ as the axial coordinate, $r=(y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, $u=(w(r),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, and require the radial field $(y,z)\mapsto w((y^2+z^2)^{1/2})$ to be $C^2$ on the closed cross-sectional disk with no slip $w(a)=0$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$w(r)=\frac{G}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2),\qquad Q_{\rm pipe}=\int_0^a2\pi r\,w(r)\,dr=\frac{\pi G a^4}{8\mu}.$$

Both fields satisfy the exact stationary Navier–Stokes equations for every choice of the positive constants and also satisfy the corresponding steady Stokes equations, because their time derivative and convective acceleration vanish. The pipe uniqueness claim uses regularity on the full disk, including the axis. Both uniqueness claims are restricted to the stated one-dimensional ansatz; neither asserts uniqueness among all flows. The domains are infinite or fully developed and give no finite entrance or exit error estimate. Under SI interpretation, $h,a,x,y,z,r$ are in metres, $u,V_0,V_1,v,w$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, $p,p_0$ in pascals, and $G$ in pascals per metre. The channel flux per unit width is in square metres per second and the pipe volume flux is in cubic metres per second.

derivations.claim: In both fields velocity has only an axial component independent of the axial coordinate; hence $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=0$. The plane momentum equation reduces to $\mu v''=-G$, and the pipe equation to $\mu(w''+r^{-1}w')=-G$ for $r>0$.

Integrating the plane equation twice gives $v(y)=-Gy^2/(2\mu)+C_1y+C_0$. The wall values determine $C_0=V_0$ and $C_1=(V_1-V_0)/h+Gh/(2\mu)$, yielding the stated profile uniquely. Its integral gives $Q_{\rm ch}$; differentiation and $\sigma_{xy}=\mu v'$ give both wall shear values.

Multiplication of the pipe equation by $r$ gives $(rw')'=-Gr/\mu$. Integration yields $w=-Gr^2/(4\mu)+C\log r+D$ on $r>0$. Full-disk $C^2$ regularity forces $C=0$, and $w(a)=0$ fixes $D=Ga^2/(4\mu)$, proving uniqueness within this ansatz. Integration with area element $2\pi r\,dr$ gives $Q_{\rm pipe}$; differentiation gives $\sigma_{rx}=-Gr/2$.

Time derivatives and convective accelerations vanish, so each field solves the stationary Navier–Stokes and corresponding steady Stokes equations for every allowed parameter choice, without a limiting or small-parameter hypothesis. This says nothing about finite-device behavior or empirical validity. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$

$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian coordinates, and fix a constant density $\rho_0>0$. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time derivatives, first spatial derivatives, and second spatial derivatives, and let $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first spatial derivatives. The formal constant-density incompressible Euler system is the pointwise system

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Use the Cartesian derivative conventions $\nabla f=(\partial_i f)_{i=1}^3$, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_i\partial_i u_i$, and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_j u_j\partial_j u$. The velocity has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives, and pressure has continuous first spatial derivatives. For this inviscid branch define the formal pressure stress by $\sigma_E=-pI_3$. On a compact oriented regular surface patch $S\subset\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, define its formal stress resultant to be $\int_S\sigma_En_S\,dS=-\int_Sp n_S\,dS$. A steady solution has $\partial_tu=0$. These definitions impose no boundary condition, assert no solution existence, and do not claim that the system describes an observed fluid.

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. $$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. These are distinct conditions. A **pathline** is a $C^1$ curve $X$ on an interval where the field is defined and the solution exists, satisfying $dX/dt=u(t,X(t))$. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. For the weak formulation, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and the restricted Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, almost-everywhere equality and integral conventions of the conservative weak-form definition. These conventions concern the weak initial data. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian coordinates, and fix a constant density $\rho_0>0$. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time derivatives, first spatial derivatives, and second spatial derivatives, and let $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first spatial derivatives. The formal constant-density incompressible Euler system is the pointwise system

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Use the Cartesian derivative conventions $\nabla f=(\partial_i f)_{i=1}^3$, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_i\partial_i u_i$, and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_j u_j\partial_j u$. The velocity has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives, and pressure has continuous first spatial derivatives. For this inviscid branch define the formal pressure stress by $\sigma_E=-pI_3$. On a compact oriented regular surface patch $S\subset\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, define its formal stress resultant to be $\int_S\sigma_En_S\,dS=-\int_Sp n_S\,dS$. A steady solution has $\partial_tu=0$. These definitions impose no boundary condition, assert no solution existence, and do not claim that the system describes an observed fluid.

For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. $$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. $$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$

Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

$$\operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI+2\mu D,\qquad \operatorname{div}\sigma+ho_0b=0.$$

Boundary, far-field, geometry and decay conditions are separate. The force-free sphere application selects $b=0$. No error estimate comparing this steady branch with the full constant-density momentum equation retaining material acceleration is asserted.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $a,\mu,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. On the exterior domain $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ put $s=U\cdot x$ and define

$$u(x)=A(r)U+B(r)sx,\qquad A(r)=1-\frac{3a}{4r}-\frac{a^3}{4r^3},\qquad B(r)=-\frac{3a}{4r^3}+\frac{3a^3}{4r^5},\qquad p(x)=p_\infty-\frac{3\mu a}{2}\frac{s}{r^3}.$$

It satisfies the steady Stokes system $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on $\Omega_a$. For $n=x/a$ on $S_a=\{x:|x|=a\}$, put $D u=(\partial_j u_i)_{i,j}$ and form the stress $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(Du+(Du)^{\mathsf T})$. The formal resultant with this sphere orientation is

$$\int_{S_a}\sigma n\,dS=6\pi\mu aU.$$

Moreover, among classical pairs $(\widetilde u,\widetilde p)$ satisfying the same Stokes system on $\Omega_a$, the same zero boundary velocity and far-field limits, and the uniform decay conditions $\widetilde u-U=O(r^{-1})$, $\nabla\widetilde u=O(r^{-2})$, $\widetilde p-p_\infty=O(r^{-2})$, this pair is unique. Here the velocity is $C^2$ and pressure $C^1$ locally up to $S_a$, the displayed bounds hold uniformly in direction, and pressure is normalized by its limit $p_\infty$. $$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. Suppose $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives; $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ has continuous first time and first spatial derivatives; and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is time-independent and $C^2$. $$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

$$ (v\cdot\nabla)v=\nabla(|v|^2/2)-v\times\operatorname{curl}v. $$

A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Suppose $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives; $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ has continuous first time and first spatial derivatives; and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is time-independent and $C^2$. Assume pointwise

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

For any reference density $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^q P'(r)/r\,dr$ for $q>0$. For a steady velocity field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$ with $u(x)$ denoting its time-independent spatial value. If $u$ and $\rho$ are independent of time, every streamline has $|u|^2/2+h(\rho)+V$ constant along it. If in addition $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component of $\Omega$, this quantity is constant throughout that component.

For any closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ satisfying $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t(t,s)=u(t,X(t,s))$, with $X_s$ and $X_{ts}$ continuous, the circulation $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$ is constant on $J$. Independently of the Euler assumptions, every $C^2$ vector field $v$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ obeys the identity

$$ (v\cdot\nabla)v=\nabla(|v|^2/2)-v\times\operatorname{curl}v. $$

No claim is made for shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative body forces, or viscous circulation. Under SI interpretation, $u$ is in metres per second, $\rho$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $P$ in pascals, and $h,V$ in square metres per second squared.

Let $h,a,\rho_0,\mu>0$, $p_0,G,V_0,V_1\in\mathbb R$, and $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. Use SI units: lengths in metres, $p_0$ in pascals, velocities in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, pressure in pascals, and $G$ in pascals per metre. Let $e_x,e_y,e_z$ be the standard Cartesian unit vectors. In Cartesian coordinates, $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_xu_x+\partial_yu_y+\partial_zu_z$ and $(\Delta u)_i=\partial_{xx}u_i+\partial_{yy}u_i+\partial_{zz}u_i$. The stress is $\sigma=-pI+2\mu D$, with $D=(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T})/2$ and $(\nabla u)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$. The selected constant-density incompressible Newtonian model has
$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

For the infinite plane channel
$\Omega_{\rm ch}=\{(x,y,z):x,z\in\mathbb R,\ 0<y<h\}$, set
$u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, with $v\in C^2([0,h])$ and wall values $v(0)=V_0$, $v(h)=V_1$. The unique profile within this one-dimensional ansatz is
$$v(y)=V_0+(V_1-V_0)\frac yh+\frac{G}{2\mu}y(h-y).$$
Its volume flux per unit width in $z$, measured in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and channel shear values are
$$Q_{\rm ch}=\int_0^h v(y)\,dy=\frac h2(V_0+V_1)+\frac{Gh^3}{12\mu},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(0)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}+\frac{Gh}{2},\quad \sigma_{xy}(h)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}-\frac{Gh}{2}.$$

For the infinite circular pipe
$\Omega_a=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ y^2+z^2<a^2\}$, take $x$ as axial coordinate, $r=(y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, $u=(w(r),0,0)$, and $p=p_0-Gx$. Require $w(a)=0$ and require the radial field $(y,z)\mapsto w((y^2+z^2)^{1/2})$ to be $C^2$ on the closed disk. The unique profile within this ansatz is
$$w(r)=\frac{G}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2),\qquad Q_{\rm pipe}=\int_0^a2\pi r\,w(r)\,dr=\frac{\pi Ga^4}{8\mu}.$$
The pipe volume flux is in $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$. For $r>0$ let $e_r=(0,y/r,z/r)$ and define the radial-axial stress component by $\sigma_{rx}=e_r\cdot\sigma e_x$; it is $\sigma_{rx}(r)=\mu w'(r)=-Gr/2$.

Both fields satisfy the exact stationary Navier–Stokes equations for every allowed parameter choice and also the corresponding steady Stokes equations because their time derivatives and convective accelerations vanish. Uniqueness is only within the stated ansätze; pipe uniqueness uses full-disk regularity at the axis. In Cartesian coordinates, $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_xu_x+\partial_yu_y+\partial_zu_z$ and $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x)$. On the punctured region $r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}>0$, set $e_	heta=(-y/r,x/r,0)$, $u=\kappa r^{-1}e_	heta$, and $p=p_\infty-ho_0\kappa^2/(2r^2)$. This steady field solves the selected unforced incompressible Euler model, is divergence-free and curl-free on its domain, and has circulation $2\pi\kappa$ around every positively oriented circle about the axis. A differentiable global potential means a single-valued $C^1$ function $\phi$ on the domain with $u=
abla\phi$; none exists.

On a connected open region, the steady solid-rotation field $u=\Omega(-y,x,0)$, $p=p_0+ho_0\Omega^2(x^2+y^2)/2$ also solves that model. A streamline here is a $C^1$ curve $\gamma:J	o\mathcal O$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval and $\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ is the selected connected open spatial region, satisfying $\gamma'(s)=u(\gamma(s))$. Its Bernoulli function $B=|u|^2/2+p/ho_0=p_0/ho_0+\Omega^2r^2$ is constant along each streamline but is not one constant across streamlines at different radii. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ on a nondegenerate real interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ (open, closed, half-open or unbounded) satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$. Here $C^1$ means that $x$ is continuous on $J$, is continuously differentiable on its interior, and at each included finite endpoint has the corresponding one-sided derivative to which the interior derivative extends continuously. The displayed equation is imposed in the interior and with that one-sided derivative at any included endpoint. The variable $s$ is a curve parameter, not time; no curve-existence assertion is made. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ nonempty and open in metres, and $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Use SI units: $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $P$ in pascals, and $V,h,B$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial derivatives, $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time, first spatial and second spatial derivatives, and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a time-independent $C^2$ potential per unit mass. Adopt the barotropic Euler equations with conservative body acceleration $-\nabla V$:
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$
For a fixed $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^qP'(r)/r\,dr$. A steady streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$. If $u,\rho$ are steady, then
$$B=\frac{|u|^2}{2}+h(\rho)+V$$
is constant along each streamline. If additionally $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component, then $B$ is constant throughout that component; here $\operatorname{curl}$ is the Cartesian curl. For every closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t=u(t,X)$, and continuous $X_s,X_{ts}$, the circulation
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$$
is constant. The conservative body acceleration and local barotropic branch are model inputs; no statement concerns shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative forcing, or viscous circulation.

In particular, take $P(\rho)=c^2\rho$ with $c>0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $V=0$, angular speed $\Omega_0\ne0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, density $\rho_c,\rho_{\rm ref}>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, angular and reference lengths $R,H$ in metres, and the open cylinder $D=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2<R^2,\ |z|<H\}$ for $R,H>0$ measured in metres. Set $r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}$, $e_\theta=(-y/r,x/r,0)$ for $r>0$, $u=\Omega_0(-y,x,0)$, and $\rho=\rho_c\exp(\Omega_0^2r^2/(2c^2))$ for $\rho_c>0$. These smooth fields satisfy both equations. For any $\ell\in(0,R)$ and $z_0\in(-H,H)$, the closed material loop $X:\mathbb R\times[0,2\pi]\to D$ is
$$X(t,\theta)=(\ell\cos(\theta+\Omega_0t),\ell\sin(\theta+\Omega_0t),z_0),\qquad t\in\mathbb R,\quad 0\le\theta\le2\pi.$$

It satisfies $X(t,0)=X(t,2\pi)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$. Its circulation is
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^{2\pi}u(t,X(t,\theta))\cdot\partial_\theta X(t,\theta)\,d\theta=2\pi\Omega_0\ell^2.$$

Its Bernoulli function is
$$B=c^2\log(\rho_c/\rho_{\rm ref})+\Omega_0^2r^2.$$
It is constant along each circular streamline but varies between radii, since $\operatorname{curl}u=(0,0,2\Omega_0)\ne0$. This is a conditional prediction of the stated smooth barotropic model, not an empirical claim about viscous flow.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. Here $C^1$ means that $x$ is continuous on $J$, is continuously differentiable on its interior, and at each included finite endpoint has the corresponding one-sided derivative to which the interior derivative extends continuously. The displayed equation is imposed in the interior and with that one-sided derivative at any included endpoint. The variable $s$ is a curve parameter, not time; no curve-existence assertion is made. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ nonempty and open in metres, and $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Use SI units: $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $P$ in pascals, and $V,h,B$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial derivatives, $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time, first spatial and second spatial derivatives, and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a time-independent $C^2$ potential per unit mass. Adopt the barotropic Euler equations with conservative body acceleration $-\nabla V$:
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$
For a fixed $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^qP'(r)/r\,dr$. A steady streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$. If $u,\rho$ are steady, then
$$B=\frac{|u|^2}{2}+h(\rho)+V$$
is constant along each streamline. If additionally $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component, then $B$ is constant throughout that component; here $\operatorname{curl}$ is the Cartesian curl. For every closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t=u(t,X)$, and continuous $X_s,X_{ts}$, the circulation
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$$
is constant. The conservative body acceleration and local barotropic branch are model inputs; no statement concerns shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative forcing, or viscous circulation.

In particular, take $P(\rho)=c^2\rho$ with $c>0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $V=0$, angular speed $\Omega_0\ne0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, density $\rho_c,\rho_{\rm ref}>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, angular and reference lengths $R,H$ in metres, and the open cylinder $D=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2<R^2,\ |z|<H\}$ for $R,H>0$ measured in metres. Set $r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}$, $e_\theta=(-y/r,x/r,0)$ for $r>0$, $u=\Omega_0(-y,x,0)$, and $\rho=\rho_c\exp(\Omega_0^2r^2/(2c^2))$ for $\rho_c>0$. These smooth fields satisfy both equations. For any $\ell\in(0,R)$ and $z_0\in(-H,H)$, the closed material loop $X:\mathbb R\times[0,2\pi]\to D$ is
$$X(t,\theta)=(\ell\cos(\theta+\Omega_0t),\ell\sin(\theta+\Omega_0t),z_0),\qquad t\in\mathbb R,\quad 0\le\theta\le2\pi.$$

It satisfies $X(t,0)=X(t,2\pi)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$. Its circulation is
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^{2\pi}u(t,X(t,\theta))\cdot\partial_\theta X(t,\theta)\,d\theta=2\pi\Omega_0\ell^2.$$

Its Bernoulli function is
$$B=c^2\log(\rho_c/\rho_{\rm ref})+\Omega_0^2r^2.$$
It is constant along each circular streamline but varies between radii, since $\operatorname{curl}u=(0,0,2\Omega_0)\ne0$. This is a conditional prediction of the stated smooth barotropic model, not an empirical claim about viscous flow.

Let $a,ho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, with lengths in metres, velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and pressure in pascals, and $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$. Define $n=x/r$, Cartesian $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_xu_x+\partial_yu_y+\partial_zu_z$, $\phi(x)=(U\cdot x)(1+a^3/(2r^3))$, $u=
abla\phi$, and $p=p_\infty+ho_0(|U|^2-|u|^2)/2$. In the selected unforced incompressible Euler model these smooth fields solve $(u\cdot
abla)u+ho_0^{-1}
abla p=0$, div $u=0$, tend uniformly in direction to $U,p_\infty$ at infinity, and have $u\cdot n=0$ at $r=a$. On the surface the velocity is $u=	frac32(U-(U\cdot n)n)$, generally nonzero tangent to the sphere. Thus the boundary is impermeable with slip, not no-slip. For the inviscid stress $\sigma_E=-pI$ and sphere normal $n=x/a$ pointing from center into exterior,
$$\int_{|x|=a}\sigma_E n\,dS=-\int_{|x|=a}p n\,dS=0.$$
This is an exact inviscid mathematical-model prediction, neither zero viscous drag nor an observed force.

derivations.claim: At $r=a$, speed is $3|U|\sin\theta/2=3\sin\theta\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Bernoulli gives $p=10^5+\tfrac12(4-9\sin^2\theta)$ Pa, yielding $100002$ Pa at $\sin\theta=0$ and $99997.5$ Pa at $\sin\theta=1$.

Pressure depends on $\sin^2\theta$ and is therefore unchanged at antipodal surface points, where normals are opposite. Their pressure-force contributions cancel in pairs; the zero result is only for inviscid pressure stress.
